item.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
item.summary: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.
item.page_text:
New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.
In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats , brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.
Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”
So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō , and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park . This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.
The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.
Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “ landmark effort ,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.
In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.
NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Yemen's Houthi rebels attack Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery - NBC News
item.summary: Satellite imagery from both NASA and Planet Labs showed thick black smoke over the installation. A satellite image shows large smoke billowing over ...
item.page_text:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s ⁠ Ras Tanura oil refinery , the kingdom’s largest, which sits alongside one of the world’s largest crude export terminals.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the refinery attack caused fires. Satellite imagery from both NASA and Planet Labs showed thick black smoke over the installation.
A source with knowledge of the matter confirmed an attack on the ⁠refinery, which covers about 230 square miles or roughly ​the ⁠size of Chicago.
The Saudi government and state oil firm Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Houthi militia, which controls much of western Yemen including the ⁠capital Sanaa , has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s ​frozen civil ⁠war reignited in July in a ‌spillover from the U.S.-Iran war .
The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or ‌cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup and ‌flagship investment conference FII.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier on Wednesday that air defenses had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. It did not say the refinery there had been struck.
Ras Tanura, which has ⁠a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, has previously been hit during the conflict with the Houthis as well as during the broader Iran war.
It is part of a complex on the kingdom’s Gulf coast that was the kingdom’s main export terminal until the U.S.-Iran war boosted the importance of Yanbu on the west coast, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline.
The Houthi spokesperson Saree had also said the group attacked Riyadh’s financial district ‌in three phases.
Saudi civil defense said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday in a ​strike on a tower in Riyadh’s financial district, the tallest building in the ‌capital that houses the headquarters of the Public ⁠Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the ⁠tower in less than a week.
The first, on Nov. 19, damaged the building but caused no injuries. The Saudi ‌civil defense posted an image ​on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some ‌damage to the building about halfway up the ​facade, similar to the impact from last week’s attack.

item.title: Mapping 25 Years of Cracks in Antarctica's Ice Shelves - Geography Realm
item.summary: A new dataset of 170 maps tracks 25 years of fractures on nine Antarctic ice shelves, including Pine Island, Thwaites, and Brunt, using Landsat ...
item.page_text:
Satellite imagery and remote sensing help researchers study some of the most remote areas of Earth. In a recent study of Antarctica, researchers used 25 years of satellite imagery to map the distribution and evolution of fractures across nine of the continent’s ice shelves.
The study, published in November 2026 in Earth System Science Data , used Landsat satellite imagery and machine learning to identify and map cracks in the ice.
Ice shelves form where glaciers and ice sheets extend beyond the coastline and float on the ocean. These floating extensions of the Antarctic Ice Sheet help slow the flow of glaciers into the ocean, a process known as buttressing.
As ice moves from the interior of Antarctica toward the coast, differences in the speed and direction of ice flow create stresses that cause the ice to fracture. These fractures include crevasses and larger cracks known as rifts, some of which extend through the entire thickness of an ice shelf . While fracturing is a natural part of the movement of ice, changes in the distribution and extent of fractures can help researchers assess the structural stability of an ice shelf.
When an ice shelf thins or retreats, it can lose some of its ability to hold back the grounded ice behind it. This allows glaciers to flow more rapidly into the ocean, contributing to sea level rise. Between 1992 and 2020, Antarctica lost about 2,671 gigatons of ice , enough to raise global sea levels by approximately 7.4 millimeters.
Although researchers have previously mapped fractures in Antarctic ice shelves using satellite imagery, there are relatively few datasets that allow them to study how these features have changed over several decades. To develop a longer historical record, researchers from Tongji University and the University of Bristol turned to the Landsat satellite imagery archive.
Get new articles on maps, geography, and the environment by email once a week. Sign up here.
Leyue Tang of Tongji University and the University of Bristol, with Jonathan Bamber, Tian Li, and Gang Qiao, used Landsat imagery to map surface damage on nine ice shelves from 1999 to 2024. The result is 170 maps at 30 meter resolution. The researchers selected nine ice shelves from different parts of Antarctica, ranging from relatively stable ice shelves to those undergoing rapid changes: Pine Island, Thwaites, Crosson, and Dotson in the Amundsen Sea sector; Scar Inlet and Brunt; and Amery, Totten, and Holmes.
Of the nine Antarctic ice shelves mapped by the researchers, Pine Island, Thwaites, and Scar Inlet experienced the most pronounced changes in surface damage over the study period.
On Pine Island, fracturing spread along the main direction of ice flow and in the shear margins, where neighboring masses of ice move at different speeds, between 2000 and 2024. The researchers associate this increase in fracturing with the acceleration of the glacier.
Pine Island’s ice shelf once shed a large iceberg every four to six years. It now calves almost every year, and the ice tends to break into smaller pieces. In February 2020, the shelf released a cluster of icebergs, only one of which, B-49, was large enough to be named.
At Thwaites, the western ice tongue broke apart, and damage on the eastern shelf is still growing. Scar Inlet, what remains of the Larsen B Ice Shelf, has kept developing new fractures since 2004.
Other ice shelves showed less change overall, but the maps still captured major events.
The overall proportion of surface damage on the Brunt Ice Shelf remained relatively stable over the study period, in part because of the large size of the ice shelf. The maps do, however, document the development of large rifts in the years leading up to major calving events.
One of these rifts, known as Chasm 1, began forming in the 1970s but remained dormant for decades before growth resumed in 2012. The growing fracture prompted the British Antarctic Survey to relocate its Halley Research Station farther inland in 2016. By early 2019, the fracture was lengthening by as much as 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) per year. The rift eventually extended beyond the McDonald Ice Rumples, an area of submerged bedrock that helped anchor the ice shelf. On January 22, 2023, a 1,550-square-kilometer (600-square-mile) iceberg known as A-81 broke away from Brunt.
While the calving of icebergs is part of the natural cycle of growth and decay of an ice shelf, distinguishing normal fluctuations from longer-term changes is difficult without an extensive historical record. As NASA glaciologist Christopher Shuman noted following the calving of A-81 , “We have no solid idea what ‘normal’ really is for this unusual ice shelf.”
One limitation of using optical satellite imagery to map fractures in Antarctica is that cracks covered by snow may go undetected, whereas radar imagery can reveal some of these hidden features. Optical imagery also restricts mapping to the sunlit months of the year. Gaps in the historical Landsat archive further limit the temporal coverage of the dataset. In 2005, for example, no Landsat imagery was acquired over the four ice shelves studied along the Amundsen Sea coast.
The Antarctic ice shelf surface damage dataset is freely available through Zenodo. The raster GIS data is available in GeoTIFF format using the Antarctic Polar Stereographic coordinate system (EPSG:3031), allowing the historical maps to be viewed and compared using GIS software such as QGIS.
Tang, L., Bamber, J. L., Li, T., & Qiao, G. (2026). A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024). Earth System Science Data, 18 . https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8591-2026
Otosaka, I. N., et al. (2023). Mass balance of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets from 1992 to 2020. Earth System Science Data, 15 , 1597–1616. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-1597-2023
